It seems as though most successful community sites tend to be founded and built upon a content-driven, discussion-focused culture. For better or worse, this sort of environment is actually conducive to the generation of interesting content, leading to a large influx of content consumption driven users. Some subset of this consumption-driven demographic want all of the content and commentary that they consume to be "safe," restricting users from openly and thoroughly discussing problematic or offensive topics. These individuals pollute and dilute the discussion, but expect the quality of the content to remain high.

Obviously, the quality of the content follows that of the discussion, as the people who produce high-effort content tend to want to discuss it thoroughly. Given that Voat is a website born of this cycle, what measures can we as a free-discussion-driven community take to ensure that the effective censorship of meme culture and the blatant censorship of social justice content consumers are unable to take root here?

I strongly disagree that service providers have an active responsibility to find and remove this content. I'm ambivalent over whether or not they should remove it once it is pointed out.

Requiring service providers to take a proactive role on things like this is impractical. It locks out smaller competitors who can't dedicate the resources to policing. It makes the company vulnerable to coordinated trolling. And, opining for a second: it demeans the users and treats them like big babies who need everything taken care of for them by someone else.

Once 'nigga house' has been found and publicized, I'm more ok with Google removing it. I don't find it racist, but then again I didn't grow up in the US; all of your racial politics confuse me. My problem is with the implication that they have a proactive responsibility to find and police this stuff before we see it
